title: Day 5 Check: Concurrency for LLD
summary: Races, locks, deadlocks and double-booking. The questions that decide senior-level signals.

questions.q: Two requests call `if (seat.isAvailable()) seat.book(user)` at the same time on a `ConcurrentHashMap`-backed repository. What happens?
options: Safe, because ConcurrentHashMap makes it atomic
A check-then-act race: both can see the seat as available and both book it. The check and the act must be one atomic step (a lock, `compute`, or CAS on the status)
questions.explain: Thread-safe collections make single operations atomic, not your sequence of operations.

questions.q: A user books seats A1, A2 and A3. A2 is taken. What should the system guarantee?
options: Book A1 and A3 and report that A2 failed
Nothing changes. Validate all seats under one lock first, then hold them all (all-or-nothing)
Retry A2 until it frees up
Book all three anyway and resolve it later
questions.explain: Partial bookings leave a mess to clean up. Validate everything, then mutate everything, inside the same critical section.

questions.q: `transfer(a, b)` locks `a` then `b`. Simultaneously `transfer(b, a)` runs. What's the standard fix for the resulting deadlock?
options: Always acquire locks in a global order (for example by account id), which breaks circular wait
questions.explain: Of the four Coffman conditions, circular wait is the one you remove in practice. `tryLock` with a timeout is the alternative.

questions.q: Why must a condition wait be wrapped in `while (!condition) cond.await()` rather than `if`?
options: Spurious wakeups happen, and another thread may consume the state change before this one reacquires the lock
questions.explain: Always recheck the predicate after waking.

questions.q: Seat holds expire after 10 minutes. Which implementation is simplest to make correct and testable?
options: Start a Timer thread per hold that releases the seat
Store `expiresAt` and treat a HELD seat with `expiresAt <= now` as available, checked lazily with an injected clock
Run a cron job every minute
questions.explain: Lazy expiry needs no background threads and no cleanup races, and tests can move time with a fake clock. A background sweeper is an optimisation you can add later.

questions.q: In Go, an elevator controller receives requests from many goroutines. Which design avoids locks completely?
options: A single goroutine owns the controller state and receives requests on a channel
questions.explain: "Share memory by communicating." Confinement to one goroutine serialises access without mutexes.

questions.q: Which collection is designed for many readers and rare writers, such as a listener list that's iterated on every event?
questions.explain: Iteration works on a snapshot and never throws. Writes copy the array, which is fine when they're rare.

questions.q: Your LRU cache uses a `ReadWriteLock` and takes the **read** lock in `get`. What's wrong?
options: Nothing. Reads should share a lock
`get` reorders the recency list (a write), so concurrent gets corrupt the linked list. It needs exclusive access
Read locks can't be held by several threads
questions.explain: An operation that reads from your API's point of view can still mutate internal state. Lock by what the code writes.

questions.q: With several app servers sharing one database, how do you stop two servers from booking the same seat?
options: A `synchronized` block in the booking service
A database guarantee: a conditional `UPDATE … WHERE status='AVAILABLE'` that checks the row count, a unique constraint, or optimistic locking with a version column
questions.explain: In-process locks only protect one process. Mention the database-level mechanism to show you can scale the design.

questions.q: Why should an observer callback or eviction callback be invoked **after** releasing your lock?
options: Foreign code might call back into your object (re-entrancy) or block. Holding your lock while it runs invites deadlocks and long stalls
Locks can't be held across method calls
questions.explain: Never run code you don't control inside a critical section.
